claims.title: Confidence is not competence
claims.statement: Feeling capable and demonstrating a skill are related but different kinds of evidence.

claims.scope: Research-informed educational explanation; no individual mechanism measurement.

limitations: Only the R13 abstract was verified; sample size, effect magnitudes, and full methods remain unverified.

sources.title: Using Neuroscience to Help Understand Fear and Anxiety
sources.summary: Theoretical review; abstract and author PDF indexed. Distinguishes defensive responses from conscious experience. Not proof of an isolated low road or this protocol.

sources.title: A Return to the Psychiatric Dark Ages with a Two-System Framework for Fear
sources.summary: Scholarly competing account, retrieved excerpts. Demonstrates substantive disagreement; do not present two-system taxonomy as universal consensus.

sources.title: Fear memories require protein synthesis…
sources.summary: Post-retrieval anisomycin disrupted later memory expression under the tested timing conditions; absent reactivation or delayed infusion did not show the same pattern. This is animal pharmacology, not evidence for self-guided imagery treatment.
sources.design: Rat fear-conditioning experiment with amygdala protein-synthesis inhibition after retrieval.

sources.title: Preventing the return of fear in humans…
sources.summary: Primary human conditioning experiment; indexed methods/results. Relevant proof-of-concept, not a universal clinical erasure procedure.
sources.correctionNote: A 2018 addendum clarified that participant inclusion/exclusion involved qualitative trial-by-trial skin-conductance assessment beyond the numerical rule originally stated. This matters when evaluating replication.

sources.title: Overview of Psychotherapy for PTSD
sources.summary: Official clinical guidance; main recommendation verified. PE, CPT and EMDR are recommended trauma-focused therapies. Does not validate a custom self-guided CPTSD PDF.

sources.title: Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach
sources.summary: Clinical/theoretical synthesis, indexed manuscript. Learning, expectancy violation and varied contexts matter; within-session calm is not the sole outcome.

sources.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
sources.summary: Official condition-specific guidance; ERP is supported. Do not treat repeated mental neutralization as general-purpose mastery.

sources.title: The causal effect of mental imagery on emotion assessed using picture-word cues
sources.summary: Emotional responses were stronger after imagery than after constructing sentences from the same cues; the second experiment manipulated processing mode. This supports an effect on emotion, not permanent memory rewriting or clinical efficacy of this method.
sources.design: Two picture–word cue experiments comparing imagery and verbal processing.
sources.population: Human adult laboratory participants; sample size not extracted.

sources.title: Imagery rescripting and EMDR…randomised clinical trial
sources.accessDepth: Publisher methods/results and abstract inspected; no independent reanalysis.
sources.summary: Clinician-rated PTSD symptoms improved during both treatments and improvements persisted to one year; the main outcome did not differ significantly by treatment condition over time. This does not establish superiority, general self-guided imagery efficacy or validation of the Sovereignty Method.
sources.design: Randomized clinical trial of imagery rescripting versus EMDR; 92 participants also had a pretreatment waiting period.

sources.title: Efficacy of imagery rescripting in non-fear emotions
sources.summary: Preregistered systematic review/meta-analysis; abstract verified: 26 studies, 1,103 participants; evidence across several negative emotions, with comparator and mechanism limits. No claim of superiority to other imagery interventions.

sources.title: No persistent attenuation of fear memories in humans: a registered replication
sources.summary: The replication found no benefit of reactivation before extinction over ordinary extinction for preventing conditioned-fear recovery. It challenges a specific human protocol, not all reconsolidation research.
sources.design: Preregistered, direct independent replication of critical reactivation–extinction conditions.
sources.population: Human laboratory fear conditioning; sample size not extracted.

sources.title: The theory of constructed emotion
sources.summary: Original theoretical account; indexed text. Useful model with testable hypotheses, not direct measurement of these autobiographical cases.

sources.title: Cognitive processes mediating behavioral change
sources.summary: Mastery-based treatment produced stronger and more generalized efficacy expectations than vicarious experience. Efficacy expectations predicted approach performance across tasks in this experiment. Not reported in the accessed abstract; do not infer a number. A specific phobia experiment, not evidence that subjective confidence equals objective skill or validates a universal self-help method. Abstract access limits appraisal of sampling, exclusions, and effect sizes.
sources.design: Treatment-comparison experiment with before-and-after efficacy expectations and approach behavior; mastery, vicarious experience, and no-treatment groups.
sources.population: Adults with phobias; exact sample size and demographics not verified from full text.

sources.title: Self-efficacy: toward a unifying theory
sources.summary: Proposes perceived self-efficacy as a contributor to starting, persisting in, and performing behavior. This is a theoretical foundation, not a trial of Sovereign Psychology. Not applicable to this theoretical paper; not a single recruited sample. Theory does not establish a literal threat-times-capacity formula, guarantee outcomes, or make felt certainty an objective measure of ability.
sources.design: Integrative theoretical account of self-efficacy and behavioral change.
sources.population: Conceptual framework drawing on behavioral-change research; not a standalone clinical trial population.

sources.title: Regulatory Flexibility
sources.accessDepth: Publisher abstract and author-hosted paper sections inspected.
sources.summary: Proposes sensitivity to context, access to varied strategies and responsiveness to feedback. This is conceptual support for a repertoire, not a trial of the website’s Perspective Rolodex.
sources.design: Theoretical review and heuristic framework; no single trial sample.

sources.title: A person-by-situation approach to emotion regulation
sources.accessDepth: Primary abstract and publisher corrigendum reviewed.
sources.summary: Greater reappraisal ability was associated with lower depression under uncontrollable stress and higher depression under controllable stress. Interpretation is context-dependent and associational.
sources.design: Individual-differences study of reappraisal ability, life stress, controllability and depressive symptoms; not randomized treatment efficacy.
sources.population: Human adults reporting recent life stressors.
sources.correctionNote: A 2016 corrigendum corrected seven participants’ depression scores and retained the substantive conclusions.

sources.title: Mind over matter
sources.accessDepth: full text: methods and discussion; publisher abstract
sources.summary: Reappraisal increased perceived resources and produced more adaptive cardiovascular responses and less negative attentional bias relative to controls. The manipulation was not designed simply to suppress arousal. 50 recruited; one withdrew and was excluded, leaving 49 for analysis. Small, short-term laboratory study in young adults. Does not establish a clinical anxiety treatment, durable cure, or causal direction between cardiovascular changes and attentional bias.
sources.design: Randomized three-condition laboratory experiment: arousal reappraisal, attention reorientation, or no instructions; public speaking and mental arithmetic stress task.
sources.population: Cambridge-area adults, 25 male and 25 female recruited; mean age 21.88; screened for specified cardiovascular conditions, medications, and pregnancy.

sources.title: Harnessing reconsolidation…meta-analysis
sources.summary: Evidence synthesis; abstract/indexed text. Include alongside later replication work, not as sole confirmation of reliable erasure.

sources.title: Prediction error governs pharmacologically induced amnesia for learned fear
sources.summary: Primary human conditioning study; abstract reviewed. Prediction error in a particular pharmacological paradigm is not a distress or self-treatment dose.

sources.title: Prediction error demarcates the transition from retrieval, to reconsolidation, to new learning
sources.summary: Primary human experiment; indexed abstract reviewed. Retrieval conditions can affect the learning process; more mismatch is not a universal dose rule.

sources.title: Subjective signal strength distinguishes reality from imagination
sources.summary: Imagined and perceived signals interacted in reality judgments around perceptual detection thresholds. These tasks do not test autobiographical memory rewriting, clinical treatment or real-world skill acquisition.
sources.population: Online adult perceptual-task participants; main analyzed online samples 272 and 339, not a single pooled study sample.

sources.title: Smaller hippocampal volume predicts pathologic vulnerability to psychological trauma
sources.summary: Primary twin study; indexed abstract reviewed. Pre-existing vulnerability is an alternative to interpreting all volume differences as trauma-caused damage.

sources.title: Not Everybody Has an Inner Voice: Behavioral Consequences of Anendophasia
sources.summary: Primary cognitive experiments; indexed abstract reviewed. Individual differences do not validate the proposed somatic treatment or establish a universal prevalence threshold.

sources.title: Baker et al. — receptor manipulation dissociates psilocybin plasticity from mouse head twitch
sources.accessDepth: Publisher indexed excerpts and Crossmark publication/currentness record; full article access redirected
sources.summary: Mouse experiment; structural remodeling and behavioral proxy do not establish human efficacy.

sources.title: Li et al. — Adjunctive fecal microbiota transplantation for major depressive disorder
sources.accessDepth: Primary abstract and conflict-of-interest statement reviewed.
sources.summary: Week-8 remission did not significantly differ; HAMD-17 reductions favored adjunctive FMT at weeks 2 and 8. Comparable tolerability in the abstract does not establish broad long-term safety or psychiatric monotherapy efficacy. The record discloses manufacturer-linked research funding.
sources.design: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled adjunctive trial; two-week FMT capsule course added to escitalopram.
sources.population: Patients with major depressive disorder; sample size not extracted.

sources.title: Li et al. — Efficacy and safety of fecal microbiota transplantation on depressive and anxiety symptoms
sources.summary: Eight studies / 532 participants, mixed RCT/cohort designs; standardized effect sizes are not percentages.

sources.title: Fu et al. — Efficacy effects of fecal microbiota transplantation on depressive symptoms
sources.accessDepth: Title/metadata identified; numerical extraction inherited from canonical register, not independently confirmed here
sources.summary: Register reports null pooled effect. Full-text reconciliation and study overlap remain open; do not select a favorable review.

sources.title: Zhang et al. — Clinical efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation in alleviating depressive symptoms
sources.accessDepth: Canonical register citation; direct PubMed retrieval returned incomplete content
sources.summary: Numerical details remain source-reported, not fresh verified extraction; reconcile included populations and overlapping trials.

sources.title: Nannan Li et al. — stressed-donor microbiota transfer in mice
sources.summary: Controlled mouse behavior/inflammation findings; not human clinical efficacy or transfer of psychological beliefs.

sources.title: FDA — Fecal Microbiota Products
sources.accessDepth: Official product index and safety-resource links
sources.summary: Regulatory context; do not extrapolate approval of products to psychiatric indications.

sources.title: NIMH — Mental Health Medications
sources.summary: Differentiate medication classes, outcomes and treatment roles; no blanket masking-versus-cure assertion.

sources.title: Dealing with feeling
sources.population: Nonclinical human samples across experimental comparisons.
sources.accessDepth: Abstract and selected full-text passages in a public article transcription; publisher blocked/paywalled
sources.summary: Effects vary by tactic and outcome. No new risk-of-bias assessment. Does not establish this lesson's efficacy. 306 experimental comparisons, not 306 people; total participant count not extracted.

sources.title: Cognitive Reappraisal and Acceptance
sources.design: Within-person sad-film experiment across two samples
sources.population: Two samples: 77 first-year US college students and 65 community adults.
sources.accessDepth: Abstract, methods and discussion in a public author manuscript
sources.summary: Reappraisal changed reported emotion more; acceptance was less difficult. Physiological difference did not replicate across samples. Laboratory tasks do not establish interpersonal transfer. Within-person sad-film task with randomized instruction order.

sources.title: Reappraisal Reconsidered
sources.summary: Unsuccessful attempts and successful emotional reduction can carry different costs; several mechanisms remain hypotheses. Narrative review; no single participant sample.

sources.title: The Impact of Acceptance Versus Control Rationales on Pain Tolerance
sources.population: Not independently verified from the accessible abstract.
sources.accessDepth: Publisher abstract only; full text paywalled, sample size and population details unverified
sources.summary: Indirect analogue for conduct while discomfort remains, not interpersonal-strategy or website efficacy evidence. Sample size and population details unverified; do not infer them.

sources.title: Learning Versus Performance
sources.accessDepth: Publisher abstract only; attempted public PDF retrieval failed
sources.summary: General learning domains, not this emotional-skills lesson; immediate performance need not establish retention or transfer. Integrative review; no single sample.

sources.title: Measuring actual learning versus feeling of learning
sources.population: Students in two Harvard introductory physics courses.
sources.summary: Immediate physics test performance and felt learning, not delayed emotional skill or real-world conduct. Randomized crossover classroom study; immediate learning outcomes.

sources.title: SCRIBE 2016 Statement
sources.design: Methodological consensus for single-case behavioral research
sources.population: Behavioral single-case research design/reporting; not an intervention sample.
sources.summary: Reporting/design guidance, not efficacy evidence for an intervention; strong controlled single-case research differs from retrospective anecdotes. Methodological consensus statement.

disciplines.title: Legitimate Authority
disciplines.learningGoal: Scope, competence, and right to act.
disciplines.practice: Choose an ordinary shared decision. List what you control, what you can influence, and what belongs to another person. Ask where consent or expertise changes your authority.
disciplines.artifact: A jurisdiction map, one corrected overreach, and a reasoned account of consent.

disciplines.title: Awareness
disciplines.practice: Record one ordinary event in five columns: observed event, bodily sensation, interpretation, urge, chosen action. Mark every inference explicitly.
disciplines.artifact: Five correctly distinguished facts and inferences with a revised entry.

disciplines.title: Understanding
disciplines.practice: Choose two explanations for one event. For each, state what you would expect to see and what would count against it. Leave unknowns visible.
disciplines.artifact: A mechanism map with rival predictions and a discriminating observation.

disciplines.title: Discernment
disciplines.practice: Find a claim you care about. Seek the strongest relevant counterevidence. Write what changed, what did not, and how your conduct will differ.
disciplines.artifact: One warranted belief revision tied to a specific change in action.

disciplines.title: Integration
disciplines.practice: Plan an ordinary conversation that calls for both firmness and care. Define one action for each, then reflect on whether both were expressed.
disciplines.artifact: A two-capacity practice record, including tensions and limits.

disciplines.title: Self-Command
disciplines.practice: Pick a manageable, low-stakes task. Choose observable conduct while allowing ordinary feelings to remain. Test it across contexts without escalating distress.
disciplines.artifact: Three contextual observations distinguishing conduct from emotional absence.

disciplines.title: Competence
disciplines.practice: Define a useful task, its performance criterion and a new context. Test it, retain failures, and teach back what the evidence supports.
disciplines.artifact: Observable performance, an acknowledged failure, and a teaching artifact.

disciplines.title: Stewardship
disciplines.practice: Plan how to notice drift, recover after a setback, and update your model. Export a record and choose your own later review date.
disciplines.artifact: A retention and recovery plan plus a dated correction record.

research.summary: H-001 [P1 | Proposed | Empirically plausible inference]. Independent threat appraisal and coping appraisal each predict emotional/physiological response to a challenging but safe event. Alternative: condition of the body, past learning and available resources explain most differences. Test: prospective vignette and controlled non-threatening task with preregistered measures of both appraisals, performance and state.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.
research.falsifier: Not yet operationalized; a source hypothesis is not an established finding.

research.summary: H-002 [P1 | Proposed | Speculative integration]. A credible, accurate reinterpretation can change an entrenched emotional response without requiring maximally intense counter-imagery. Alternatives: habituation, attentional shift, passage of time, goal disengagement, demand effects, context. Test: compare structured meaning-change rehearsal and active credible control in a low-risk nonclinical context.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.
research.falsifier: Not yet operationalized; a source hypothesis is not an established finding.

research.summary: H-003 [P1 | Proposed | Empirically plausible inference]. Vivid mental imagery can elicit physiological emotion, yet induced intensity does not linearly predict useful updating. Falsifier: across adequate replications, intensity alone outperforms content credibility and behavior in safe tasks. Safety: do not deliberately induce extreme distress; limit self-training to manageable nonclinical tasks.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.
research.falsifier: Not yet operationalized; a source hypothesis is not an established finding.

research.summary: H-004 [P1 | Proposed | Speculative integration]. The Identity-to-Competence Loop improves follow-through above information or affirmation alone when it includes objective field tests. Distinguish expectation, actual task skill and confidence calibration. Design: compare education-only, imagery-only, behavior-only and combined groups when ethically feasible.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.
research.falsifier: Not yet operationalized; a source hypothesis is not an established finding.

research.summary: H-005 [P1 | Proposed | Empirically plausible inference]. Diverse perspective-selection skill and feedback-sensitive switching predicts stronger adaptive transfer than rigid reliance on one preferred self-state. Test: rotating task contexts with blinded assessment of appropriateness, outcome and strategy switching.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.
research.falsifier: Not yet operationalized; a source hypothesis is not an established finding.

research.summary: H-006 [P1 | Proposed | Speculative integration]. Conviction contributes to performance and autonomic response independently of proposition accuracy and skill. Threat of confounding: self-efficacy may partly reflect real skill and previous victories. Measure factual calibration, confidence, actual prior skill, expectancy and performance separately.
research.nextStep: Specify population, comparator, observable endpoint and disconfirming evidence before a study. No study is underway through this website.

research.summary: H-007 [P2 | Proposed | Speculative integration]. Allowing naturally arising unfamiliar emotion without self-identification, then choosing conduct, can reduce secondary emotional struggle. Test: distinguish naturalistic emotional observation from suppression, self-criticism and rumination. Strong claims require validated scales and prospective data.

research.summary: H-008 [P2 | Proposed | Speculative integration]. The severity of an expectation violation changes the credibility and specificity of corrective evidence needed for transfer, but does not imply that stronger subjective distress is always more effective. Competing predictions: optimal learning depends on surprise, safety, controllability, context, retrieval and retention.

corrections.text: “Conscious understanding and automatic defensive responses can diverge. Learning involves interacting brain systems; cognitive and behavioral approaches can change responses.”
“Threat processing, bodily responses and conscious fear are related but distinguishable. No single brain region explains the full experience.” Label diagrams conceptual.
“Learning can change responses through several processes. Reconsolidation is one investigated account, with boundary conditions.”

Replace attack table with intervention scope, evidence and limitations. “Evidence-based therapies can develop durable skills and reduce symptoms. The Sovereignty Method is not yet validated as a standalone treatment.”
“Rehearsal should be relevant and manageable. Evaluate what was learned and whether it transfers; intensity alone does not establish benefit.” No mandatory arousal slider target.
“Repeat when it adds useful learning, vary context, and reassess. There is no established universal repetition count for this framework.” Count may log activity, never certify neural updating.
“A field test can assess behavior and transfer. It cannot by itself identify the memory mechanism.” No ‘reconsolidated’ completion state.
Explain inhibitory learning and reconsolidation as distinguishable accounts with overlapping practical questions. Assess durability and return of fear; do not promise erasure.
Replace with educational field guide. No self-administered trauma protocol, clinical efficacy badge or implied equivalent to established therapy.
Distinct personal observations must remain distinct from one another and from measured mechanisms. No private case narrative is published here.
“Some components have research support. The integration, personalization and proposed mechanisms remain open to testing.” Link claim-level evidence.
Correct citation to Nader, Schafe & LeDoux; describe rat fear-memory experiment and protein-synthesis intervention. Do not present it as an imagery trial.
“Expectations can shape anxiety alongside actual circumstances, bodily state, learning history and other factors.” Predictive processing is an explanatory framework.
“Constructionist theories emphasize prediction, concepts and bodily signals. Other accounts emphasize different mechanisms.” Explain predictions and limits, not a winner badge.
“Approach and defensive tendencies may change, but anger, confidence and fear can coexist.” Do not use dominance as the default corrective state.
“Imagery can evoke emotion and share processes with perception; overlap does not make imagined and real events equivalent.”
“Credibility, specificity, context and meaningful feedback may matter; prediction error is not the same quantity as distress.” Keep H-008 open.
Separate factual support, subjective conviction, expected ability and observed performance. A failed test can appropriately lower confidence.
“Sovereignty develops through truthful perception, chosen conduct, recovery and correction; feelings may remain.” Keep no-emotion ideals in philosophical context only.
Retrospective reports have multiple possible explanations and cannot identify a causal mechanism. Detailed personal narratives are withheld.
Optional presentation preferences can be tested; no inferred brain type, clinical matching or diagnosis.
Do not offer a thought-neutralization workflow. Provide conceptual education and condition-specific care context.
Label historical; omit arousal targets and root-cause detector. Use behavior, functioning, adverse effects and uncertainty. Retain 1/4/12-week checks only as proposed checkpoints.
Define metaphors explicitly. Keep spiritual teaching and empirical claims separately navigable and separately tagged.
Threat estimates and perceived coping capacity can both matter. Show them separately; do not calculate an anxiety score or claim a literal neural equation.
Memory updating has boundary conditions. This interface cannot detect a reconsolidation window and provides no timer or universal five-hour prescription.
Imagery and perception can share processes while remaining distinguishable. Motor simulation findings do not demonstrate efficacy of this intervention.

Research examines brain systems involved in learning and regulation. No imaging or physiological study of this protocol establishes repaired temporal tagging, hippocampal restoration, or structural strengthening.
Record intensity descriptively if useful, never as a required target or proof of memory updating. Reassess usefulness, functioning and unwanted effects without escalating to satisfy a number.
Offer text, planning, role-play and optional imagery. These are accessibility choices; their relative benefit in this framework remains to be tested. Omit uncited population percentages.

No breathing, cold-water, forced-arousal or confrontation protocol is prescribed by this educational interface. Ordinary behavioral planning can be offered without claiming autonomic override or guaranteed reciprocal inhibition.
Worsening, no benefit and inconclusive results are valid outcomes. Pause, reassess the premise and consider alternatives; do not assume more repetitions will produce permanent change.
Choose a usable rehearsal format. Whether combining formats improves transfer is an empirical question; more modalities are not automatically better.
Personal reports can generate questions. Evaluating efficacy requires an appropriate prospective design, outcomes, comparison, and reporting of nonresponse and adverse effects.
Separate structural plasticity, subjective experience, useful learning and clinical outcomes.
The recalled quantitative FMT source claim remains unresolved. No numerical efficacy claim is published.
Describe acute symptom regulation, function, relapse and maintenance separately; distinguish SSRIs and benzodiazepines.
Report design-specific findings and uncertainty; do not convert SMD/g to percentage improvement or treat adjunctive results as monotherapy.

takeaways.title: Separate the two questions
takeaways.text: What do I expect will happen? What support or skill could help me respond? Keep these judgments separate rather than calculating an anxiety score.

takeaways.title: Describe a state, not your whole self
takeaways.text: Try “I am noticing anxiety about this conversation.” A feeling can be important without defining your character or deciding your next action.

takeaways.title: Look for ordinary evidence
takeaways.text: Choose a small, safe action that can tell you more about your prediction. Record what happened, including outcomes that did not fit your expectation.

videos.example: Before a routine email: “I expect my question will annoy them.” Draft a clear, respectful question; send it if appropriate, then record the actual reply rather than guessing its meaning.
videos.action: Write one prediction and one resource. Choose a respectful question you can ask in an ordinary situation.
videos.reflection: What did I predict, what actually happened, and what remains uncertain?

videos.evidenceNote: Imagery can be a rehearsal tool, but this companion does not prescribe intense threat imagery, repetition quotas, or a ten-minute nervous-system reset. Do not relive trauma or push through escalating distress; persistent or severe symptoms deserve qualified support.

takeaways.title: Choose one situation
takeaways.text: Replace “be more confident” with a specific, ordinary moment: asking a question, starting a task, or expressing a preference.

takeaways.title: Name the prediction and your options
takeaways.text: Write the feared outcome separately from the resources you can use: preparation, a clear sentence, time, or help.

takeaways.title: Measure action, not perfect calm
takeaways.text: Notice what you did and how daily functioning changed. A useful action can count even when some discomfort remains.

videos.example: For a routine meeting, write and briefly practice: “Could you clarify the deadline?” Use it when relevant; afterwards note whether you asked, what response you received, and anything you would adjust.
videos.action: Write one useful sentence. Practice briefly in a comfortable format, then use it when appropriate.
videos.reflection: Did rehearsal help the action, or did I need a different kind of support?

videos.title: Learn the science without overpromising
videos.platformTitle: Why This Works: The Neuroscience of Rewiring Your Nervous System
videos.summary: Use learning research to ask better questions about change—and keep mechanisms separate from proof that a particular method works.
videos.transcriptStatus: Complete automatic English captions reviewed; source moments linked. Captions may contain transcription errors.
videos.rights: Original upload retained. Captions are not redistributed.
videos.evidenceNote: Laboratory research on imagery and memory updating does not establish guaranteed fear erasure, a universal five-hour window, or this video’s exact protocol. Retrieval-extinction findings have replication limits; greater emotional intensity is not a proven shortcut.

takeaways.title: Compare expectation with observation
takeaways.text: The video explores prediction-based accounts of learning. In everyday practice, record an expectation before an action and compare it with what you actually observe.

takeaways.title: Use rehearsal as preparation
takeaways.text: A short imagined or written practice can help organize your next step. Follow it with real-world feedback rather than treating imagined success as demonstrated skill.

takeaways.title: Ask what a study actually tested
takeaways.text: Distinguish a laboratory learning finding from evidence for a complete self-help protocol. Notice the participants, task, outcome, and limits before applying a claim to your life.

videos.example: Before asking for feedback, write “I expect only criticism.” Afterwards list the words you actually heard. Separate your interpretation from the observable response.
videos.action: Before one ordinary action, note your prediction. Afterwards, record observable evidence separately from interpretation.
videos.reflection: What would count as evidence against my first interpretation?

videos.title: Adapt the practice—not your worth
videos.platformTitle: Why the Protocol Isn’t Working Fix These 5 Failure Modes
videos.summary: Troubleshoot the target, format, and real-life usefulness of a practice without blaming yourself or escalating distress.
videos.transcriptStatus: Complete automatic English captions reviewed; source moments linked. Captions may contain transcription errors.
videos.rights: Original upload retained. Captions are not redistributed.
videos.evidenceNote: No fixed arousal band or minimum repetition count has been established here. These alternatives are accessibility options, not proven equivalent routes to reconsolidation. Stop if an exercise becomes overwhelming; nonresponse is not personal failure.

takeaways.title: Clarify the meaning you are predicting
takeaways.text: Ask “What am I expecting, and what would it mean to me?” Treat the answer as a hypothesis—not a diagnosis or proof uncovered by a strong body sensation.

takeaways.title: Use an accessible format
takeaways.text: If mental pictures are difficult, try a written outline, spoken sentence, or simple role-play for an ordinary task. You do not need vivid imagery to make a practical plan.

takeaways.title: Let results change the plan
takeaways.text: Record whether the practice helped you do something useful. No improvement is information: revise, pause, or seek support rather than assuming you need more force.

videos.example: If visualizing a presentation is unhelpful, write the opening sentence and say it aloud once. Ask a trusted person whether the message is clear; revise from that feedback.
videos.action: Choose a specific task and a usable format. Try a small action, then pause to review whether it helped.
videos.reflection: Was the target specific, was the format useful, and did the action become easier to carry out?

videos.title: Build self-direction and meaningful connection
videos.platformTitle: Re-upload: Sovereign Psychology As the Cure to Loneliness Epidemic.
videos.summary: Explore agency, competence, and connection together—without treating loneliness as a personal defect.
videos.transcriptStatus: Complete automatic English captions reviewed; source moments linked. Captions may contain transcription errors.
videos.evidenceNote: Self-determination theory includes relatedness alongside autonomy and competence. This companion presents reflection and connection practices, not a cure for loneliness or proof that needing others is a weakness.

takeaways.title: Keep autonomy and connection together
takeaways.text: The discussion names autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Ask which need is least supported today rather than assuming independence means needing nobody.

takeaways.title: Make a little space before reacting
takeaways.text: Notice and name what you are feeling before choosing a response. The purpose is choice, not suppressing emotions or withholding support from yourself.

takeaways.title: Turn a value into a small action
takeaways.text: Choose a concrete action that reflects the person you want to be: keep a modest promise, practice a skill, or reach out with a genuine invitation.

videos.example: Choose a manageable task you care about, then message someone you trust with a specific invitation to talk or meet. Both self-direction and support can belong in the same day.
videos.action: Choose one modest promise to yourself and one genuine invitation to connect with someone you trust.
videos.reflection: What do I need right now: rest, a useful action, contact, or a combination?

videos.title: Choose a response that fits the situation
videos.platformTitle: The Sovereignty Method: How to Rewire Fear at the Nervous System Level
videos.summary: Move from a vague threat story to a specific situation, a realistic response, and feedback you can use.
videos.transcriptStatus: Complete automatic English captions reviewed; source moments linked. Captions may contain transcription errors.
videos.evidenceNote: The video presents a proposed method. The companion keeps the practical planning elements without endorsing guaranteed rewiring, universal dosing, or a validated reconsolidation protocol. Clinical anxiety or trauma needs individualized care.

takeaways.title: Make the target concrete
takeaways.text: Describe the setting, the outcome you expect, and the response you want to practice. Choose an everyday situation, not a traumatic memory.

takeaways.title: Match the response to the need
takeaways.text: A helpful response may be curiosity, a boundary, compassion, or preparation—not dominance. Choose what is appropriate to the actual situation.

takeaways.title: Test usefulness in real life
takeaways.text: After a manageable action, record what happened and whether your response helped. Treat confidence as a feeling to compare with behavior, not proof of competence.

videos.example: If routine feedback feels like rejection, prepare: “Which part should I improve first?” Ask when appropriate and note the specific guidance you receive.
videos.action: Name the situation, choose a fitting response, and identify what observation would change your plan.
videos.reflection: Did my response meet the situation’s needs, and what would I do differently next time?

videos.title: Start now. Build the habit over time.
videos.platformTitle: Skip the "66-Day" Habit Loop: How to Reprogram Instantly
videos.summary: Make the next action deliberate while allowing automatic habits to develop through repeatable practice.
videos.transcriptStatus: Complete automatic English captions reviewed; source moments linked. Captions may contain transcription errors.
videos.evidenceNote: An immediate decision is not the same as an automatic habit. Lally and colleagues found widely varying habit-development times; 66 days was a sample median, not a rule. This companion does not use the video’s shock, hyperventilation, or aversion instructions.

takeaways.title: Name one concrete behavior
takeaways.text: Replace “stop wasting time” with a visible target, such as putting the phone away when you begin a chosen task.

takeaways.title: Notice the urge without attacking yourself
takeaways.text: Describe the feeling or urge neutrally, then choose your next action. This companion uses observation—not disgust, shame, or distress induction.

takeaways.title: Track what you actually do
takeaways.text: Record the cue, the action you took, and what made it easier or harder. Adjust the environment and repeat a manageable alternative.

videos.example: “When I sit down to write, I will put my phone out of reach and write one rough sentence.” Track attempts for a week to learn what helps—not to prove that a habit has been permanently installed.
videos.action: Choose a stable cue and a small replacement action. Make the environment support it and record each attempt without judging your worth.
videos.reflection: What cue helped me start, and how can I make the next attempt easier?

models.title: Appraisal & self-efficacy
models.focus: How demands and perceived resources shape approach.
models.prediction: Changing perceived coping resources may alter choices while external demands stay the same.
models.limits: Self-efficacy can reflect prior skill. No individual physiology calculator.
models.evidence: Component experiments and foundational theory; integrated product not assessed.

models.title: Inhibitory learning
models.focus: New learning competes with an earlier response across contexts.
models.prediction: Context and retrieval cues can affect whether a learned response returns.
models.limits: Within-session calm is not sufficient evidence of durable transfer.
models.evidence: Clinical and theoretical synthesis; new product not assessed.

models.title: Reconsolidation
models.focus: Retrieved memories may become susceptible to modification under particular conditions.
models.prediction: Retrieval conditions can alter later expression of a learned response.
models.limits: Retrieval alone is insufficient; replication and boundary conditions matter.
models.evidence: Animal and human experimental paradigms; individual mechanism not assessed.

models.title: Constructionist accounts
models.focus: Concepts, predictions and bodily signals contribute to constructed experience.
models.prediction: Context and learned concepts may influence experienced emotion.
models.limits: A theoretical account with competing explanations; not universal consensus.
models.evidence: Theoretical accounts and scholarly disagreement; clinical integration not assessed.
